processing: Partially oxidised by withering and tossing, then fixed, rolled and dried, as with other Dancong.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most high-mountain Dancong.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight, plump strips of a yellow-brown colour with an oily sheen.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: A high, clean natural floral aroma with the mountain character of Wudong; the body is mellow, refreshing and lightly sweet, with a strong sweet return.

brewing.notes: Short steeps to start, as with any Dancong; lengthen once the sweetness arrives.

vintage_note: As is usual for named Dancong, it is sold by harvest year and season, mostly fresh spring tea or tea rested a year or two after roasting. Leaf from one old tree can only be scarce, so a large supply under this name deserves a question.
description:
Baishuweng is a named Dancong from Wudong in the Fenghuang mountains. The name points to the tree's yellow-green foliage rather than to its aroma, which sets it apart from the many Dancong named for a scent.

It follows ordinary Dancong steps: withering, tossing, fixing, rolling and drying. The result is a plump, straight, yellow-brown strip with an oily shine.

The liquor is golden, and the cup combines a high natural floral aroma with the mountain character Wudong tea is prized for, mellow and refreshing with a strong sweet return.

It is often mentioned among the famous old trees of Wudong, which makes it an easy name to borrow. Ask for the tree and the village, and be wary if the seller cannot answer.
history: A Chinese account of famous Wudong trees places it at about 1100 metres in a garden at Zhongxinyan village and gives the tree an age of over 300 years. That age has not been independently confirmed. Who first selected it is not recorded.
